chapter_theme: At the start of Civakan's departure for the ascetic's life, his wives weep and reproach his shoulders, chest, tongue, eyes and crown and recall the loves that brought him to them, and the palace and city fall into a silence of grief.

cast.role: the hero, now preparing to renounce his kingdom
the wives of Civakan, who lament his leaving; individual speakers are not named in the Tamil

2949.reading: The wives, speaking to the jewelled shoulders of their lord, recall the favour he showed their painted feet and ask whether the shoulders will now embrace them or stand hard of heart.
2949.nuance: They address his body parts, not him; the lament runs through shoulders, chest, tongue, eyes and crown in the verses that follow. The sense of the second line is hard to fix.
2949.event: Civakan's wives reproach his shoulders as he prepares to leave them.

2950.reading: Speaking to the chest where pearls and wreaths lay, the wives say that if the old friendship is dropped, that chest is no longer the refuge it was.

2951.reading: The wives remind the chest that it pressed their breasts in love and ask whether he will now cast them off and not look at them once he rules the earth.
2951.event: The wives accuse him of leaving them for his rule.

2952.reading: The wives say the tongue that praised them as swan, peacock, lute and nectar has shown two tongues, and call him, like a king, pitiless and hard.
2952.event: The wives reproach his tongue for its broken praise.

2953.reading: The wives tell his eyes that they cared for their breasts and gave them great joy, and now, eyeless, do not see the state they are in.

2954.reading: The wives tell the jewelled crown that it looked on their smiles and now looks on the loss of their lives, and bid it 'live long' in bitter irony.
2954.nuance: The 'long life' is an irony; the crown that once took their feet now sees them destroyed.
2954.event: The wives reproach his crown with bitter blessing.

2955.reading: The wives cry that the sea of milk has turned to poison, the sun has borne darkness and the moon pours fire, and ask how they can hold their lives, calling on the gods.
2955.event: The wives cry out that the world has turned against them.

2956.reading: The speaker asks whether the woman of the long eyes, named Gandharvadattai, is a heavenly maid or a Vidyadhara girl, and asks who will now take up the music she knew.
2956.nuance: The addressees and speaker are not fixed by the Tamil; the verse may be a wife's plea about Gandharvadattai or Gandharvadattai's own.
2956.event: One wife turns her lament to Gandharvadattai and the music they shared.

2957.reading: A wife promises to kill the long-eyed Gunamalai, who was caught by the elephant and was rescued when he killed it and embraced her, and asks whether she too is of that kind now.
2957.nuance: The verse reminds him of the rescue to show what he owes; the threat to kill is more likely a cry of despair than a plan.
2957.event: A wife recalls the elephant's attack on Gunamalai and his rescue.

2958.reading: A wife recalls Padumai, whom the snake bit and who revived when he took her coral mouth as nectar, and asks whether the venom has now come back on them.
2958.event: A wife recalls the cure of Padumai.

2959.reading: A wife reminds him that her eyes pierced his chest through the sandal paste and asks whether he will let that joy, once gained, go.
2959.event: A wife recalls their first love and asks him not to leave it.

2960.reading: A wife says that he who raved over their eyes, lips and bodies, and showed his bow, now gives them up like a rag laid on a wound, and asks if renouncing is worth anything.
2960.nuance: Here the wives put renunciation as a question of what is fitting; the Naladiyar and Kural praise it as the best course.
2960.event: A wife questions the worth of his renunciation.

claims.claim: renouncing those who love is not a thing of worth

2961.reading: A wife says that those who entered the golden city's street and were caught in the net of a dancing woman's long eyes now find that the light has gone and ask whether the wreath is a pain.
2961.event: A wife recalls how he was caught in love's net.

2962.reading: A wife says that he who delighted in the one like a lotus, guarded by women, and joined her as a brahmin with music, is wrong to give them up, and asks if renouncing is fitting.
2962.nuance: It recalls the episode in which Civakan came as a brahmin; the wife it names is not fixed by the Tamil.
2962.event: A wife recalls his stay as a brahmin and asks if renouncing is fitting.

claims.claim: a husband who took a wife's love ought not to forsake her

2963.reading: A wife says that he, strong-shouldered and the killer of enemies, drank and danced with Lakshmanai before all, and asks whether he will leave in affection while others tremble.
2963.event: A wife recalls how Civakan danced with Lakshmanai.

2964.reading: The palace, with sobbing women worshipping him and weeping in every direction, becomes like a deep sea, as even stones and trees melt.
2964.nuance: The verse moves from the wives' own words to the narrator's sight of the whole palace in grief.
2964.event: The women of the palace weep and worship him as he prepares to go.

2965.reading: Some women beat their golden bangles, scatter garlands and tremble like caught does, asking whether the king will guard their lives or leave them unguarded.
2965.event: The women strip off ornaments and weep as the king departs.

2966.reading: The women, weeping with faces like water-lilies, are like jewelled flags on a mast that tremble and cry.
2966.event: The women cry out in grief.

2967.reading: The drums, the lutes, the flutes and the tinkling anklets all fall silent, and the king's palace is as if dead.

2968.reading: Great tuskers, war-horses and the rest stand silent and shed tears, taking no food, in the palace of the departing king.

2969.reading: Women, having cast off earrings, bangles, wreaths, sandal and jewels, make the palace look like a sky robbed of stars, as if the golden world had moved out.

2970.reading: The king's city, rich in jewels and gold, is stirred like the sea churned for nectar.

2971.reading: The kitchens, almshouses and halls, once rich in ghee, rice and savoury, now stand as if every living breath had gone from the town.

2972.reading: The costly rice, the sweet dishes and the curd lie wasted on the empty street, since those who wanted them are not there.

2973.reading: The cup of wine in the youth's hand is untouched, the maids leave their jewels and garlands, and sandal and pearls lose their beauty.

links.note: 2957 recalls the rescue of Gunamalai from the elephant, which 1068 shows Civakan teasing her about in the early love.
links.teaches: The wives hold his old rescue against him, so a joke between lovers turns into a debt called in at the parting.

links.note: 2958 recalls Padumai restored after the snake bite that 1285 shows him curing with his spells.
links.teaches: The cure that made him a hero is cited as the proof that his love gave life, so leaving takes it back.

links.note: 2951 has the wives ask whether he will cast them off, while 1097 has him say he will not melt in grief and that even a sesame-seed of attachment is a fault.
links.teaches: His own earlier teaching to weeping women is now turned on him by wives who ask for what he then refused to grant.

links.note: 2962 asks whether a husband may give up the wife he took, while Naladiyar 56 says a husband cannot easily put away a wife even if she lacks good qualities.
links.teaches: The wife's plea is that the bond cannot be cast off, which the Naladiyar says too but only to praise those who avoid marriage.

gains.a: the wife's plea that a husband is bound gains the support of a rule from the moral literature that she does not cite
gains.b: the Naladiyar's argument that marriage binds hard gains a case where the bond is felt by those left, not by the husband

links.note: 2960 asks whether renouncing wives can be worthy, while Naladiyar 53 says the best renounce home, youth and beauty without delay.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's praise of the best renouncers leaves out the people left behind, whom the wives put forward as the cost.

gains.a: the wives' question is given the opposing view that the best of men renounce what they love without delay
gains.b: the Naladiyar's praise of renouncing gains the weeping wives that its list of things given up does not name

links.note: 2965 shows the wives stripping bangles and weeping at the king's going, while Tirumanthiram 157 has the wives and kin who wailed turn back at the town's edge.
links.teaches: The epic shows grieving women at a living man's leaving, where the Tirumanthiram shows the same women turning back at a dead man's bier.

gains.a: the wives' grief gains a Saiva reading in which wives, kin and children turn back at the edge of town
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's turning back gains a living scene where the same grief ends in a king's choosing to go

links.note: 2964 and 1104 both show women beating and weeping at the going of Civakan, once into prison and now into renunciation.
links.teaches: The same hero's leaving is wept over twice, first as a captive and then as one who goes freely.

source_issues: Verses 2949-2955 and 2967-2973 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2956-2963 do not name their speakers and several wives are named only as the lovers recalled, so speakers are given as the wives as a group.
Many lines of 2949-2955 are hard to parse and are marked uncertain.
